À l’occasion du Mois de l’histoire des N: For Black History Month, La Converse sits down with Nancy Oliver-MacKenzie.

For Black History Month, La Converse sits down with Nancy Oliver-MacKenzie. She comes from one of Nova Scotia's historic Black communities, rooted in the region since the 17th century, and has lived in Montréal for more than 50 years. She is dedicated to sharing and preserving chapters of history that are often overlooked. Nancy Oliver-Mackenzie is an early riser.
« Je peux dormir et me lever quand je ve: “I can sleep and get up whenever I want, but I like going to the window and watching the sky before the sun comes up,” says the elder, describing her life in her Notre-Dame-de-Grâce home, where she lives alone but is well surrounded. Now retired, the former teacher and community organizer is nowhere near slowing down.
Ce qui l’allume, c’est la découverte de: What lights her up is discovering history: a family history that goes back to slavery in the 1800s, and the forgotten Black history of her adopted city, Montréal.
« Lorsque ma mère est décédée en 1991, j: “When my mother died in 1991, I inherited a family photo album I had never seen,” she says. The images, some of which date back to the 1920s and 1930s, show what life was like in Nova Scotia at the time. “They tell a wonderful story,” says Nancy.
« Je veux les numériser pour les préserv: “I want to digitize them to preserve them and share this history.” It is one of her many projects. The album set her off on a search for her origins, a long-haul effort that demands an enormous amount of time and work.
À chaque séjour dans sa province natale,: Every time she goes back to her home province, Nancy combs through archives and registries and deciphers documents on microfilm. That is how she found Moses, her paternal great-great-grandfather. He and his family, who were enslaved, fled Maryland for Nova Scotia during the War of 1812. “He worked on a tobacco plantation. With his wife, an enslaved domestic worker, and their 14-month-old daughter, he took a boat to Nova Scotia. They settled near Halifax.
La suite appartient à l’histoire », raco: The rest is history,” Nancy says. Life in the Maritimes was perilous at first. “They were given land where it was hard to grow anything. They struggled for several generations before they were really doing more than surviving.”
Elle partage une réflexion qui lui a tra: She shares a thought that crossed her mind the very morning of our conversation: “I wish people could understand how many pioneers there have been in our history, and what we owe to their perseverance, their tenacity, their vision,” she says. “Can you imagine being on a tobacco plantation, hearing about a place called Canada, and having a vision of the future, despite all the risks?
Ils ont dû réfléchir à tout ça, tout en: They had to think all of that through while being held in slavery,” she says. Today, it is hard to imagine such a life, under the especially gruelling conditions of tobacco farming. “I find it incredible that they were able to marry, have a child, and find a way to get to the boat.”
On s’imagine alors un jeune père de fami: One pictures a young father of 30, his 18-year-old wife and their one-year-old baby slipping away in the light of morning, crossing the vast countryside on foot toward the ocean. Nancy is still tracing her maternal ancestors.
Son grand-père maternel fut le seul offi: Her maternal grandfather was the only Black officer commissioned during the First World War. She has a copy of the journal he kept during the war. In it, he mentions letters he wrote to his wife and his 9-year-old daughter – Nancy's mother – the racist incidents Black soldiers endured, and also the unity among the soldiers at the front.
« Une des choses merveilleuses [dans le: “One of the wonderful things [in the journal] is the trusting relationship between these men, who were so close,” she says. “It's not very detailed, but you can read between the lines.” The son of an enslaved person himself, her grandfather came directly from the United States to live in Nova Scotia. “There is so much to discover,” she adds.
<strong>L’éducation au cœur de la commun: Education at the heart of the community
Nancy s’installe à Montréal en 1967 avec: Nancy moved to Montréal in 1967 with a university degree in early childhood studies in hand. Wary of the public school system of the time, she first chose to become a stay-at-home mother to raise her two children. Along the way, she earned a teaching degree from McGill University and began a career as a teacher. Her children attended the elementary school that would become FACE, of which she is one of the founding parents.
« Le directeur avait mis en place beauco: “The principal had set up a lot of extracurricular activities: music, art, theatre, and outings,” she recalls. “The parents and the administration wanted to make it all more formal by founding an alternative school.”
L’école voit le jour en 1975.Ses enfants: The school opened in 1975. Once her children were grown, a desire to see the country led Nancy to teach in Inukjuak, a village in Northern Quebec. She then headed to southern Africa, where she taught in Botswana and Eswatini.
Après quelques années à l’étranger, Nanc: After a few years abroad, Nancy settled back in Montréal. Hungry for change, she left teaching for community work. “The public school system wasn't particularly stimulating or interesting, and it didn't really meet all of children's needs.
J’ai pensé que je pourrais peut-être fai: I thought maybe I could do more outside that system,” she says. She was then living across from the NDG Black Community Centre, where she first got involved as a volunteer. She went on to work there for several years. “I realized it wasn't only about the children, but about the adults too.
Il y a des façons de se réunir et de se: There are ways of coming together and supporting one another that don't depend on the system. We have to work from where we are, rather than having something imposed on us,” she believes. Nancy speaks glowingly of the organization, which no longer exists. “Black community centres haven't survived in this millennium. I don't really understand why,” she laments. Several institutions have indeed closed their doors, while others have changed their mission.
Elle cite le Negro Community Centre of M: She cites the Negro Community Centre of Montreal (NCC), a Little Burgundy heritage institution founded in 1927, of which she was a member. The centre, which welcomed a visit from Nelson Mandela in 1990, among others, ceased operations around the turn of the 2000s. A group of citizens wants to bring the historic centre back to life with a museum and community centre project.
« Ma philosophie est que nous avons vrai: “My philosophy is that we really need to stick together, to collaborate and work together in a way that avoids this kind of situation,” she says. “We have to do everything we can to stay together and not see these centres disappear.”
Femme au grand cœur, Nancy a pris part à: A woman with a big heart, Nancy has been part of several communities. “You can have your own community, no matter where you settle,” she believes. For nearly 30 years, she has been a member of the Union United Church of Montreal, a historic Montréal church. “When I came back from Africa in the early 1990s, I really needed to feel at home, with Black people,” she says of her immersion in African culture.
« Montréal ressemblait à une mer de visa: “Montréal looked like a sea of white faces. It was really hard to adjust to a totally white environment. I wanted to feel more comfortable,” she recalls. Union United Church, located where downtown, Saint-Henri and Little Burgundy meet, is the oldest Black congregation in Canada. It was founded in 1907 by Black parishioners who faced racial discrimination in white churches. Nancy is busy preserving the institution's rich history <l1>through a website</l1>.
« Je mets des biographies, des photos, d: “I put up biographies, photos, newspaper articles, you know, everything I can find,” she explains. She hopes to be able to pick the project back up after the pandemic. With her research, she also wants to highlight the contributions of Black women, who are too often forgotten. “I really feel like there are so many unsung heroes, especially women,” Nancy says. “I'm particularly interested in them. It's hard to track down the documents.
On entend souvent parler de celles qui s: You often hear about the ones who are in the public eye, but you don't hear about some of those who had an enormous influence on a lot of people. That's what really interests me. Many women did a lot of volunteer work and helped the community. And their stories need to be told, just like those of the well-known people,” she believes.
Elle recense également plusieurs musicie: She is also documenting several Montréal jazz musicians who have often never been heard of. They are artists to discover, or rediscover, such as pianist Ilene Bourne. Nancy loves film and reading, and we can only hope that her stories will soon be there to read or watch. A publisher once took an interest in her military grandfather, but she doesn't want to tell her family story halfway. “For me, it wasn't enough,” she says. “After all, it's who I am.”
